title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 11: Digitizing Law Schools
keywords: Rule 112 of the Rules of Court
first line of defense against injustice
primary_topics: Chapter 11 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- the address CJP delivered to launch the Supreme Court's e-library simultaneously in eight law schools and universities nationwide, opening the Court's electronic library to law professors and law students in order to make the study of law 'easier, more convenient and more systematic.'

The e-library is presented as the Court's direct answer to the 'I' in CJP's ACID agenda -- incompetence and gross ignorance of the law -- which he documents with the Court's own recent discipline of six lawyers and six judges in a single month.

A survey of the technology program supporting the reform: computer orientation courses for the Supreme Court and appellate courts and then for 2,000 judges and 26,000 employees, an easy-payment laptop acquisition scheme, affordable DSL at home, the PhilJA Development Center in Tagaytay funded by a P300 million Japanese grant, and the full computerization of the Sandiganbayan as the model for the whole judiciary.

The closing thesis that technology is only as good as the people who use it, and that law schools -- not the courts -- are the country's first line of defense against injustice, so digitizing them is itself judicial reform.
sub_topics: The simultaneous launch at Arellano University School of Law, simulcast live to Aquinas University in Legazpi, Saint Louis University in Baguio, Silliman in Dumaguete, University of San Carlos in Cebu, Xavier in Cagayan de Oro, Ateneo de Davao and Mindanao State University in Marawi.
The e-library's pedigree: first of its kind in Asia and one of the few in the world, conceived and developed in under a year at a minimal cost of US$10,000 granted by the World Bank.

A nostalgic contrast between legal study then and now -- waiting for barely readable mimeographed copies of decisions and writing one's own digests, against pressing a few keys to have a case pop out of the screen and electronically cutting and pasting a digest for recitation.

CJP's assumption of office as Chief Justice on December 21, 2005, his pledge to continue the APJR begun by CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr., the four Ins, and the ACID code name for the judiciary's four problems.

Evidence of incompetence on the bench: in January alone the Court sanctioned six lawyers and six judges, one judge found grossly ignorant of the law for delaying the preliminary investigation of two child-rape cases and allowing the child to be cross-examined in violation of Section 3 of Rule 112.

The e-library's history under Justice Antonio T. Carpio -- launched November 19, 2004 for the justices, officials and employees of the Supreme Court, continually updated, and distributed to lower-court judges on compact discs pending full computerization.

What the e-library holds: decisions and resolutions, circulars and administrative issuances, the Rules of Court, manuals and bench books, laws, the National Administrative Register, journals and law lists -- a judge's database and 'a formidable arsenal of legal knowledge.'

The five reasons the e-library is unique: it is cheap, always up to date (decisions uploaded within 48 hours), accessible seven days a week, needs no space, and is fully searchable by word, phrase, case title, number, subject, date, parties and ponente.

The training and equipment program: basic computer orientation starting with the Supreme Court and appellate courts and spreading to 2,000 judges and 26,000 employees, easy-term laptop purchases, and affordable home DSL -- leaving magistrates 'no more excuse' for failing to keep abreast of law and jurisprudence.

Two other anti-incompetence projects under the APJR: the PhilJA Development Center in Tagaytay City, made possible by a P300 million grant from the Japanese government and envisioned as an ASEAN center of judicial excellence; and the full computerization of the Sandiganbayan by March 2006 as the model for the entire judiciary.
The concluding exhortation to law professors and students to use the e-library as a cost-effective research tool and to digitize their law schools in aid of speedy, accurate and quality justice.

stances.claim: Incompetence and gross ignorance of the law on the bench and in the bar are alarming developments that must be abated at once, and the e-library is a concrete institutional answer to them rather than a mere convenience.
stances.rhetorical_move: diagnosis-then-remedy: naming incompetence as one of the four ACID problems, proving it with the Court's own recent disciplinary record, then presenting the e-library and the computerization program as the cure

stances.claim: With the e-library, computer literacy courses, easy-term laptops and home DSL in place, magistrates have no more excuse for failing to keep abreast of current laws and jurisprudence or for failing to act on motions and decide cases.
stances.rhetorical_move: removal-of-excuses: pairing each stated obstacle to e-research with a program that removes it, so that the remaining fault is personal rather than institutional

stances.claim: Law schools, not the courts, are the first line of defense against injustice, so opening the Court's e-library to professors and students is itself an act of judicial reform.
stances.rhetorical_move: relocating the front line: shifting responsibility for the quality of justice upstream from the bench to legal education, which justifies sharing a court-built tool with the schools

stances.claim: Technology alone cannot reform the judiciary, because new tools can only be as good as the people who use them.
stances.rhetorical_move: qualifying his own showcase: conceding the limits of the very innovation he is launching in order to pivot to the human formation that must accompany it

notable_anecdotes: CJP recalls his own student days, when the only way to get a copy of a decision was to wait for a mimeographed duplicate that 'took time to make' and was 'oftentimes not too readable,' and the best way to digest cases was to write them out by hand.

He describes the modern student's experience with visible amusement -- press a few keys and 'presto, the case pops out of the screen,' after which an electronic cut and paste leaves the digest done and the student ready for recitation.

He recounts the disciplinary case of a judge found grossly ignorant of the law, who failed to conduct the immediate preliminary investigation of two child-rape cases and allowed the child victim to be cross-examined and humiliated during the investigation.
He notes the e-library's origin story as a point of institutional pride: the first of its kind in Asia, built in less than a year for only US$10,000 from the World Bank.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduces the address Chief Justice Panganiban gave to launch the Supreme Court's electronic library simultaneously in eight law schools and universities -- Arellano University School of Law, with a live simulcast to Aquinas University in Legazpi, Saint Louis University in Baguio, Silliman in Dumaguete, the University of San Carlos in Cebu, Xavier in Cagayan de Oro, Ateneo de Davao and Mindanao State University in Marawi. He noted that the e-library was the first of its kind in Asia and one of the few in the world, conceived and developed in less than a year for only US$10,000 granted by the World Bank, and that sharing it with the schools was meant to make the study of law easier, more convenient and more systematic. He contrasted the study of law in his own time, when students waited for barely readable mimeographed copies of decisions and wrote their own digests, with a present in which a few keystrokes bring a case onto the screen. He then tied the project to his program: on assuming office on December 21, 2005 he had pledged to continue Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr.'s Action Program for Judicial Reform, to lead a judiciary marked by four Ins -- integrity, independence, industry and intelligence -- and to attack the ACID problems of limited access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence and delay. Citing the Court's discipline of six lawyers and six judges in a single month, including a judge found grossly ignorant of the law in two child-rape cases, he presented the e-library, developed under Justice Antonio T. Carpio and launched on November 19, 2004, as the remedy for incompetence: cheap, updated within 48 hours, always open, space-free and fully searchable. He described computer orientation courses reaching 2,000 judges and 26,000 employees, easy-term laptop purchases, home DSL, the P300 million Japanese-funded PhilJA Development Center in Tagaytay, and the Sandiganbayan's full computerization as the model for the judiciary. Conceding that new technologies 'can only be as good as the people who use them,' he argued that law schools, not the courts, are the first line of defense against injustice, and exhorted professors and students to digitize their law schools.
